answer: The crowd re-runs its ledger every close and writes each fault it turns up, a row that will not reconcile or a tally that will not add up, on a slate at the inlet of the ledger. A head is paid for closing one open fault for good, and the slate is struck so no second head can claim it. Real faults arrive only as the crowd's own history breeds them, never on demand, so an honest sparrow takes the shallow ones while a farm's tenth head must wait for the ledger to dig deep, and a head may not wander off with a fault it cannot prove, for a false one burns the finder's bond for good.
